power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: We report how we determined our sample size, all data exclusions (if any), all manipulations, and all measures in the study. A total of 153 participants (84% women, Mage = 20.9 years) were recruited from the Queen's University SONA Participant Pool during January The sample size was determined using a power analysis with G*Power (Faul et al., 2009), drawing from a partial eta squared (ηp²) of .062 derived from Krzyś et al. (2025), which was based on an interactive effect of Spatial Certainty and Distractor Placement on attentional guidance. This effect size was converted to Cohen's f (f = 0.257). Given the input parameters (f = 0.257, α = .05, power (1-β) = .95), the computed required sample size was 52. However, as we expected an interaction between Spatial Certainty and Placement, we increased the sample size to 104 participants. This decision was based on guidelines for achieving sufficient statistical power for detecting interactions, which typically require larger sample sizes due to the complexity and smaller effect sizes associated with interaction effects (Lakens & Caldwell, 2021). Additionally, given that the experiment was conducted online, we anticipated a high dropout rate (Rodd, 2024; Zhou & Fishbach, 2016). This further justified the decision to recruit a larger sample to maintain sufficient statistical power.

We report how we determined our sample size, all data exclusions (if any), all manipulations, and all measures in the study. There were 94 participants recruited from the Drawing from a previous study, Castelhano and Heaven (2011) reported a significant main effect of location consistency on eye movements with an F-value of 26.21, which converts to a large effect size (Cohen's f = 1.32). To be conservative and ensure robustness, we used an effect size of f = 0.4 for our power analysis, reflecting a medium to large effect size commonly seen in eye movement studies related to spatial consistency (e.g., Malcolm & Henderson, 2010).

Using the effect size f = 0.4 and considering the need to detect an ordinal interaction effect, we doubled the sample size based on guidelines from Lakens and Caldwell (2021). Given the input parameters (f = 0.4, α = 0.05, power = 0.95), the computed required sample size was approximately 20 participants. Multiplying by 4 to account for interaction effects (Lakens & Caldwell, 2021) resulted in a total sample size requirement of 80 participants.

(2025), which was based on an interactive effect of Spatial Certainty and Distractor Placement on attentional guidance.

To ensure stimuli were presented at the same size regardless of the size of the screen, participants were instructed to take out a credit card or equivalent and scale an image on their screen using the arrow buttons on their keyboard to match the size of the credit card (standard size of 5.398 cm high by 8.56 cm wide).
Participants were instructed to click the fixation cross to begin the trial and were shown the scene without the critical object for 2 seconds.
Participants were instructed to identify whether object name matched the masked object (right or left).
Participants completed three practice and 48 experimental trials.
After briefly viewing the critical object, participants were then asked to identify whether the object under the black box by clicking the object's name (in this example, a dustpan or a powerstrip).

Participants were recruited solely through the Queen's University SONA Participant Pool, a closed institutional system restricted to enrolled undergraduate students who have authenticated accounts, and this Experiment was not listed on any other open recruitment platform.

The design of the experiment, such as scaling the display against a physical credit card using arrow keys, and use of clicks in specific areas, and key presses ensured that participants had a high degree of investment in the study and were following the instructions needed to complete the task.

For Reaction Time, we observed significant main effects of both Placement and Spatial Certainty: participants were slower to respond to objects in Unexpected Placements and to Low-Certainty objects overall.

There were 94 participants recruited from the Drawing from a previous study, Castelhano and Heaven (2011) reported a significant main effect of location consistency on eye movements with an F-value of 26.21, which converts to a large effect size (Cohen's f = 1.32).
All participants were instructed to indicate whether the object named at the beginning of the trial matched the critical object, with a 1:1 ratio of signal-to-noise trials.
After obtaining consent, participants were given the task instructions before being calibrated on the eye tracker.
Participants were asked to fixate on the red dot, and upon doing so, the critical object appeared in the parafoveal vision of the dot, 4° away (Castelhano & Pereira, 2018).
Each participant completed three practice trials and 48 experimental trials.

Although Experiment 2 employed a different response format (Yes/No) than Experiment 1, comparable accuracy levels across experiments suggest that participants were similarly able to perform the recognition task and provide a stable basis for examining the effects of spatial certainty and placement on recognition performance.
Overall average discriminability was high across conditions (Figure 6A), indicating that participants were generally able to identify objects successfully.
In the present task, participants were directed toward a predefined target location, reducing the opportunity for spatial certainty to influence gaze allocation.
All participants gave informed consent before participating.
Queen's University SONA Participant Pool and were compensated with a course credit or $18 per hour during September 2024 to April 2025.
All participants had normal or corrected-tonormal vision and did not participate in Experiment 1.

text.text: Observers use high-level knowledge to support object recognition, including expectations about object locations.
However, these expectations are not uniform: some objects have precise object-location priors, whereas others have more flexible spatial distributions.
Across two experiments collected in 2024-2025, we examined how the precision of object-location priors shapes object processing by manipulating spatial certainty and object placement within scenes.
Experiment 1 used an online two-alternative forced-choice recognition task, and Experiment 2 used a gaze-contingent paradigm to examine processing across fixations.

Recognition accuracy and sensitivity showed a significant interaction between spatial certainty and placement: highcertainty objects benefited from expected placement and were impaired by unexpected placement, whereas low-certainty objects showed weaker placement effects.
In contrast, eye movement measures in Experiment 2 showed broad effects of placement, but no interaction with spatial certainty.
These findings suggest contextual prediction in scenes is graded, objectspecific, and temporally distinct across visual processing and recognition.
People do not recognize objects based only on visual input; they also use knowledge about where objects are likely to be found in the world.
Across two experiments, we found that this knowledge matters most for objects whose locations are highly predictable.
When an object's location is more flexible, and therefore, less predictable, then the recognition of the object is less affected by its location.
Interestingly, we found that when we examined processing using eye movements, unexpected placements mattered for all objects.
These findings may help explain why misplaced objects differ in how they affect performance and slow visual decisions in everyday tasks only in some cases.
For instance, finding a tool in a messy garage versus spotting the stop lights while driving.
The apparent ease with which we understand the visual world around us belies the complexity of underlying processes.

Current theories of perception suggest that visual processing is fundamentally predictive, with incoming sensory input continuously evaluated against expectations derived from prior knowledge and recent experience (Clark, 2013; Keller & Mrsic-Flogel, 2018; Rao & Ballard, 1999).

text.text: In scenes, these expectations are not only semantic, but also spatial: observers know where objects are likely to appear.
Critically, the precision of these object-location priors varies across objects.
Some objects are strongly tied to a particular region of a scene, whereas others can plausibly appear in several locations.
The Spatial Certainty Index captures this variability by quantifying the strength or precision of learned object-location regularities (Krzyś et al., 2025).
text.formatted: The Spatial Certainty Index captures this variability by quantifying the strength or precision of learned object-location regularities <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Krzyś et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Objects high in spatial certainty have higher spatial precision, belonging to a specific region of a scene (i.e., a chandelier is in the upper region), while objects low in spatial certainty have more distributed spatial distribution.

In the present study, we examined how spatial certainty (as reflective of the precision of object-location priors) shapes object recognition processes, and whether this influence emerges during visual processing or later recognition decisions.

This question follows directly from predictive-processing accounts, in which prior knowledge constrains perception by weighting incoming sensory evidence against expectations derived from experience (Rao & Ballard, 1999; Peelen et al., 2024).
text.formatted: This question follows directly from predictive-processing accounts, in which prior knowledge constrains perception by weighting incoming sensory evidence against expectations derived from experience <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Rao & Ballard, 1999;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Peelen et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Applied to object recognition in scenes, this raises two possibilities.
For an early-integration account, precise spatial priors should influence object processing as visual information is first sampled and integrated across fixations.

Under this account, high-certainty objects should show the strongest benefit from expected placement and the greatest cost from unexpected placement in eye movement measures, particularly those sensitive to parafoveal and early foveal processing.

For a later evidence-evaluation account, spatial priors may instead exert their strongest influence after initial object information has been sampled, when observers need to evaluate visual evidence and map it onto a decision of the object's identity.

Under this evidence-evaluation account, placement and spatial certainty may both affect eye movements, but their interaction should most clearly emerge in behavioural measures, such as accuracy and signal detection sensitivity.
Eye movements provide a useful way to distinguish these accounts because object recognition in scenes unfolds across successive fixations.

High acuity information is available only near the center of fixation (~2° from the center), so observers must use extrafoveal information and scene-based expectations to guide processing before and during fixation (for review, see Rayner, 2009).

text.text: A key issue concerns how information sampled across successive fixations is combined into a coherent perceptual representation.
Research has shown that information acquired parafoveally (~4°-5° of visual angle from center) on one fixation can be integrated with foveal input in the next (Rayner, 1998; Rayner et al., 1978).

text.text: Gaze-contingent paradigms provide direct evidence that visual information acquired before fixation can influence subsequent processing once its been directly fixated.
This was first shown in a seminal study where Rayner (1975) introduced the Boundary Paradigm.

text.text: This involved placing an invisible boundary before a preview word in a sentence and changing the visual information once the boundary is crossed by an eye movement.

Subsequent work showed that preview benefits depend on the relation between the preview and the target, as well as the predictability of the target word is within the sentence context can benefit its processing (Schotter, Angele & Rayner, 2012; Veldre & Andrews, 2018).

text.text: This model partitions scene layout into upper (e.g., ceilings and upper walls), middle (e.g., tabletops and countertops), and lower (e.g., floors and lower walls) regions, reflecting systematic vertical regularities in object placement.

Objects with high spatial certainty are strongly associated with a single region (e.g., clouds in the upper region), whereas objects with low spatial certainty are associated with multiple possible regions (e.g., plants).
Importantly, it is not the case that low-certainty objects have no expected location or no spatial associations, rather the spatial associations are more distributed.
In predictive processing terms, spatial certainty can be understood as indexing the precision of an object-location prior.

In the present experiments, high-certainty objects appeared either in the region where they are typically expected or in a region that violated that expectation; low-certainty objects were included to test whether placement effects depend on the precision of the object-location prior.
So, if the precision matters during object processing, high-certainty objects should be especially affected by whether they appear in expected or unexpected locations.
The unresolved question is when this effect emerges: during object processing across fixations, or during later evidence evaluation and recognition decisions.
The present study tested whether the precision of object-location priors influences object processing across fixations, recognition decisions, or both.

text.text: What remains unclear is whether the precision of these spatial priors alters the integration of object information across fixations or whether it emerges when observers evaluate visual evidence and make a recognition decision.
Across two experiments, we manipulated spatial certainty and object placement in a fully crossed design.
Experiment 1 examined whether spatial certainty constrains recognition decisions when objects appear in expected or unexpected scene regions.
Because the response alternatives differed in spatial certainty, this task was designed to test whether participants used spatial priors when evaluating limited visual evidence.
Experiment 2 examined whether these spatial priors also influence object processing across fixations by using a gaze-contingent paradigm and eye movement measures.
These experiments tested between two theoretical accounts of the effects of precision of spatial priors on object processing and recognition.

The early-integration account predicts a Spatial Certainty × Placement interaction in eye movement measures, with expected placement facilitating and unexpected placement disrupting processing most strongly for high-certainty objects.

Critically, this facilitation should be evident not only after fixation of the target object, but also during the fixation immediately preceding target fixation, when parafoveal information is first extracted.

The later evidence-evaluation account predicts a different pattern: placement and spatial certainty may each influence eye movements, but their interaction should emerge most clearly in behavioural measures of recognition accuracy and sensitivity.
Experiment 1 tested whether the precision of spatial priors influences recognition decisions when objects appear in expected or unexpected scene regions.
It provided the necessary foundation for examining how these spatial associations influence eye movements and processing in Experiment 2.

Critically, the distractor presented in the 2AFC task was semantically consistent with that scene context but was the converse level of Spatial Certainty (Low-Certainty distractor with High-Certainty target and vice versa).
This response structure is important for interpreting the task.

Because the foil was semantically consistent with the scene but differed from the target in spatial certainty, the decision required participants to evaluate briefly presented object information in relation to the spatial plausibility of the two alternatives.
Thus, Experiment 1 was intended to assess recognition decisions under spatially constrained evidence.

As Experiment 1 was administered online, several features of recruitment and task design were implemented to limit automated or non-genuine responding.

Participants were recruited solely through the Queen's University SONA Participant Pool, a closed institutional system restricted to enrolled undergraduate students who have authenticated accounts, and this Experiment was not listed on any other open recruitment platform.

The design of the experiment, such as scaling the display against a physical credit card using arrow keys, and use of clicks in specific areas, and key presses ensured that participants had a high degree of investment in the study and were following the instructions needed to complete the task.
Finally, we removed three participants who performed under 75% accuracy, leaving a total of 150 participants for the analysis.
This exclusion criterion was used to ensure the reliability of the data by excluding participants who may not have been fully engaged with the task or may have misunderstood the instructions.

Because the theoretical interpretation of Experiment 1 depended on whether Placement and Spatial Certainty interacted, we supplemented the frequentist analyses with Bayesian model comparisons.

Bayes factors quantify the relative support for competing models and were useful here because the non-significance in our frequentist analysis does not provide evidence in favour of the null model (Kass & Raftery, 1995; Dienes, 2014; Faulkenberry, 2025; Faulkenberry, Ly, & Wagenmakers, 2020).

Bayes factors were computed using the BayesFactor package (Morey et al., 2024) in R with the lmBF function.

The additive model was favoured over the interaction model, BF 𝑎𝑎𝑎𝑎𝑎𝑎/𝑖𝑖𝑖𝑖𝑖𝑖 = 2.80, ±2.34%, providing weak evidence that reaction time was better characterized by separable effects of Placement and Spatial Certainty than by the interaction.
This result is consistent with the frequentist analysis, in which Placement and Spatial Certainty independently slowed responses, but did not interact.

For accuracy, the interaction model was strongly favoured over the additive model, BF 𝑖𝑖𝑖𝑖𝑖𝑖/𝑎𝑎𝑎𝑎𝑎𝑎 = 6.94 × 10 16 , ±3.0%, indicating overwhelming evidence that accuracy was better characterized by a Placement × Spatial Certainty interaction than by additive main effects alone.

For discriminability, we used the same model-comparison approach as above, with a comparison of an additive model containing the main effects of Placement and Spatial Certainty with an interaction model that also included the Placement × Spatial Certainty term.
Because d′ was computed at the participant × condition level, candidate models included random intercepts for participants only.

The interaction model was strongly favoured, BF 𝑖𝑖𝑖𝑖𝑖𝑖/𝑎𝑎𝑎𝑎𝑎𝑎 = 1.61 x 10 13 , ±1.93%, indicating that, like accuracy, discriminability was better characterized by the Placement × Spatial Certainty interaction.
Together, the Bayesian analyses support the same pattern as the frequentist results.
Placement and Spatial Certainty contributed largely additively to response speed, whereas their joint influence emerged strongly in recognition accuracy and discriminability.

This pattern is consistent with the later evidence-evaluation account, which states that the precision of objectlocation priors most clearly constrained recognition decisions when participants evaluated briefly presented object evidence.
Experiment 1 investigated whether the precision of spatial priors, as measured by spatial certainty, affected recognition decisions under limited visual evidence.
The 2AFC task was designed to assess recognition decisions when sensory evidence was limited, and the scene's spatial information remained available.
Because the foil was semantically consistent with the scene but differed from the target in spatial certainty, participants could not solve the task based on scene semantics alone.
Instead, decisions required evaluating the briefly presented object evidence against the spatial plausibility of the response alternatives.

For High-Certainty targets, Expected Placement may have supported the target decision, whereas Unexpected Placement may have weakened support for the target and made the Low-Certainty foil relatively more plausible.
Conversely, for Low-Certainty targets, performance may have depended partly on whether the High-Certainty foil was spatially plausible or easy to reject.

Thus, the Experiment 1 effects are best interpreted as evidence that spatial certainty constrains recognition decisions when limited object evidence must be evaluated against the spatial plausibility of the response alternatives.
We expected participants to recognize High-Certainty objects in Expected Placements faster and more accurately because the placement of these objects aligned with strong objectlocation priors.
In contrast, we expected smaller or absent placement effects for Low-Certainty objects because their spatial associations are more flexible and distributed.
The results partially supported these predictions.

For Reaction Time, we observed significant main effects of both Placement and Spatial Certainty: participants were slower to respond to objects in Unexpected Placements and to Low-Certainty objects overall.
However, the interaction was not significant and the Bayesian model comparison provided weak evidence for the additive model over the interaction model.
Thus, the RT data do not allow a firm conclusion about whether Placement and Spatial Certainty act additively or interact.

In contrast, both Accuracy and Discriminability (d′) revealed significant Placement × Certainty interactions, suggesting that the influence of spatial placement on recognition was modulated by the object's spatial certainty.
Bayesian model comparisons strongly supported this pattern, with the interaction model strongly favoured for both accuracy and discriminability.
As predicted, High-Certainty objects were recognized more accurately and with greater sensitivity when they appeared in Expected locations.
This pattern is consistent with the idea that precise spatial priors constrain how briefly sampled object evidence is evaluated during recognition decisions.
For Low-Certainty objects, Placement did not significantly affect discriminability.
Numerically, however, performance did not show the same Expected-Placement advantage observed for High-Certainty objects.

One possible explanation is that the spatial plausibility of the foil influenced recognition decisions, such that the High-Certainty foil may have been easier to reject when it was spatially implausible.
Thus, the interaction should be interpreted as evidence that spatial certainty did change the diagnostic value of placement during recognition.
Taken together, these findings emphasize the importance of considering object-level spatial certainty when examining the role of context in visual recognition.
They also raise important questions about when these effects arise during processing.
Accuracy and sensitivity suggest that spatial priors constrain recognition decisions, whereas reaction time suggests that Placement and Certainty contribute independently to processing speed.
The Bayesian analysis weakly favoured this dissociation by favouring an additive account for reaction time but interaction models for accuracy and discriminability.

As such, Experiment 1 cannot determine whether spatial certainty alters processing as information is sampled across fixations or whether its strongest effects emerge during later evidence evaluation and recognition decision processes.
To address this, Experiment 2 used eye tracking to examine whether spatial certainty influences object processing across fixations.

By analyzing eye movement measures, Experiment 2 tested whether the behavioural benefits observed in recognition accuracy and sensitivity also emerged during parafoveal and foveal object processing, or whether they were most clearly seen in later recognition decisions.
This allows for a more complete understanding of how spatial expectations guide object recognition in real-world scenes.

In Experiment 2, we investigated whether spatial object-scene associations influence the integration of visual information across fixations, as object information is sampled parafoveally and then processed after direct fixation.

To do so, we used the gaze-contingent paradigm (Castelhano & Pereira, 2018) to limit the availability of visual input across fixations and examine the extent to which top-down spatial expectations influence processing.

text.text: If the early-integration account is correct, then precise spatial priors constrain object processing across fixations.
In this case, high-certainty objects should show the strongest benefit from expected placement and the greatest cost from unexpected placement in eye movement measures.

This effect should be evident in measures reflecting parafoveal and early processing once the object has been directly fixated (such as the pre-target fixation, and the first fixation and gaze duration measures).
In contrast, low-certainty objects should show weaker placement effects because their spatial priors are more distributed and so the placement effects should be smaller or absent.
Alternatively, if the later evidence-evaluation account is correct, then placement and spatial certainty may each affect eye movements without necessarily interacting.

In this case, the Placement x Spatial Certainty interaction should emerge most strongly in the behavioural measures, such as accuracy and sensitivity, when observers evaluate the available visual evidence and make an explicit recognition decision, as in Experiment 1.

text.text: The experiment followed a 2 (Placement: Expected or Unexpected) by 2 (Spatial Certainty: High or Low) within-subjects design.
All participants were instructed to indicate whether the object named at the beginning of the trial matched the critical object, with a 1:1 ratio of signal-to-noise trials.
The same stimuli from Experiment 1 were used for Experiment 2.
Eye movements were tracked using an EyeLink 1000 + (SR Research) sampling at 1000 Hz.
The stimuli were displayed on a 21" cathode ray tube (CRT) monitor with a 100 Hz refresh rate at 800 x 600 pixels resolution, subtending 25° x 33° of visual angle.
Viewing was binocular, but only the right eye movements were recorded.
After obtaining consent, participants were given the task instructions before being calibrated on the eye tracker.
Participants sat 60 cm away from the monitor with their heads positioned on a chin rest.
After adjustments to the head and chin rest, they were calibrated using a 9-point calibration screen.
Calibration checks with a 5-point calibration screen occurred after every trial to ensure that the eye tracking error was low.
The experimenter recalibrated the system if any fixation exceeded .5° from the checkpoint.
First, a name cue was shown for 2 seconds, followed by a fixation cross for 500 ms.
Next, the background scene (not containing the critical object) appeared for 450 ms, followed by a red dot.
Participants were asked to fixate on the red dot, and upon doing so, the critical object appeared in the parafoveal vision of the dot, 4° away (Castelhano & Pereira, 2018).

text.text: Once the participant fixated the object region (rectangular boundary of 1° from the centre of the target) for 60 ms, the critical object disappeared (Rayner et al., 2003).

text.text: Because the object disappeared, the eye movement measures reflect, at least partly processing, after object offset.
The participants indicated via button press whether the critical object matched the object shown at the beginning of the trial (by pressing the "a" key) or did not match (by pressing the "l" key).
Each participant completed three practice trials and 48 experimental trials.
The experiment lasted about 45 minutes.

In Experiment 2, we examined both eye movement and behavioural performance measures to assess how spatial associations influenced object processing across fixations and subsequent recognition decisions.
Eye movement measures provide a temporally sensitive window into object processing as information is sampled parafoveally and after the object is directly fixated.
Behavioural measures index how available visual evidence is evaluated when participants make a recognition decision.

To characterize object processing over time, four standard measures were computed within Regions of Interest (ROIs) defined as a 2° rectangular border around the target object's outermost edge: Pre-target Fixation, First Fixation Duration (FFD), First Gaze Duration (FGD) and Total Time (TT).
The pre-target fixation was defined as the as the fixation during which the critical object appeared parafoveally.
Because the critical object was only available parafoveally during this fixation, Pre-target fixation duration provides an index of processing before direct fixation of the object.

This measure was included to test whether spatial certainty influenced object processing at the earliest point in the trial sequence, when object information could be sampled parafoveally but before the object was fixated.

For the present framework, the Pre-target fixation is particularly relevant to the early-integration account, which predicts that precise spatial priors should modulate processing before the transition to direct fixation.

FFD reflects the length of the first fixation on the object and is commonly interpreted as reflecting early object processing and initial object parsing after direct fixation (Nuthmann et al., 2010; Rayner, 2009; Williams & Castelhano, 2019).
text.formatted: FFD reflects the length of the first fixation on the object and is commonly interpreted as reflecting early object processing and initial object parsing after direct fixation <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Nuthmann et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Rayner, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Williams & Castelhano, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Shorter FFDs index more efficient early processing, whereas longer FFDs suggest increased or more difficult processing.

In the present framework, FFD is informative because an early-integration account predicts that the precision of spatial priors should modulate object processing immediately after it is initially fixated.
FGD, defined as the sum of fixation on the ROI during the first entry, reflects continued processing and integration of object information.
In the present paradigm, visual information from the object disappeared 60ms after fixation onset.
Thus, FGD likely reflects not only processing of the available visual input, but also the continued evaluation of briefly sampled object information in relation to scene context expectations.
TT represents the sum of all fixations on the ROI and provides a more global measure of object processing that includes refixations and later viewing.
Longer TT is typically associated with increased difficulty processing object identity or integrating the object with the scene context.
TT is not an early measure, but it reflects whether the interaction between placement and spatial certainty emerges during extended object processing before the explicit response.
For all eye movement measures, trials more than ±3 standard deviations from each participants' own mean were excluded (~1.78% of data excluded).
As in Experiment 1, behavioural performance was assessed using Accuracy and Discriminability (d′).

These measures were central to testing the later evidence-evaluation account, which predicts that the Placement × Spatial Certainty interaction should emerge most clearly when participants evaluate the available visual evidence and make a recognition decision.

We also computed the signal detection measures: response bias, Criterion (c) and Bias (log β) because they can help determine whether the behavioural effects reflect sensitivity versus response tendencies.

We first report the eye movement measures to examine whether spatial certainty and object placement influenced object processing across fixations.

Measures are presented in temporal order: pre-target fixation duration, when the critical object was available parafoveally; first-fixation and first-gaze duration, which reflect early processing after direct fixation; and total viewing time, which reflects more extended viewing and reinspection.

This sequence allowed us to test whether the Placement × Spatial Certainty interaction appeared in eye movements, as predicted by the early-integration account, or whether eye movements showed separable effects of placement and spatial certainty, as predicted by the later evidence-evaluation account.

Instead, it suggests that any influence of spatial certainty was not expressed in the timing of the fixation immediately preceding target fixation.
Thus, although spatial certainty did not appear to alter pre-saccadic fixation duration, it may still influence processing after direct fixation or during later recognition decisions.

This pattern suggests that unexpected placement increased processing time during the first fixation on the object.

However, the absence of a Placement × Spatial Certainty interaction provides little support for the early-integration account at this stage: High-Certainty objects did not show a larger Expected Placement benefit or Unexpected Placement cost than Low-Certainty objects.

First Gaze Duration (FGD) was defined as the sum of all fixations on the critical object during its initial viewing, and Total Time (TT) was defined as the sum of all fixations on the object across the entire trial.

FGD is commonly interpreted as indexing initial object processing and integration of object information, whereas TT reflects more global processing associated with resolving object identity and integrating the object within the broader scene context (Castelhano & Pereira, 2018; Castelhano & Rayner, 2009; Rayner, 2009).

The consistency of this pattern across FGD and TT suggests that object placement influenced both initial and extended viewing of the target object.
However, the absence of Placement × Spatial
Certainty interactions indicate that this placement effect was not detectably modulated by the precision of the object-location prior.

This pattern is more consistent with the later evidenceevaluation account than with the early-integration account: spatial placement influenced eye movements broadly, but the specific interaction between placement and spatial certainty was not evident in object-viewing durations.
Across the eye movement measures, we did not observe the predicted Placement × Spatial Certainty interaction in which expected placement selectively benefited objects high in spatial certainty.

Pre-target fixation duration showed no reliable effects of placement or spatial certainty, suggesting that these factors did not measurably influence processing before the target object was directly fixated.
Once the object was fixated, however, object placement did exert influence on processing measures across levels of spatial certainty.
Objects in unexpected locations were viewed longer than objects in expected locations, and critically, this cost was not detectably modulated by the precision of the object-location prior.
Thus, this pattern provides little support for the early-integration account in eye movements.
However, we return to this issue below using Bayesian Factors to compare whether the data best warrants an additive, or an interaction model.

We next examined whether the interaction emerged in behavioural measures of recognition accuracy and sensitivity, as predicted by the later evidence-evaluation account, which reflects decision-making and evidence accumulation (Antes, 1974; Henderson et al., 1987; Peelen et al., 2024).

To further characterize how spatial certainty and object placement influence object recognition, we also examined signal detection measures of discriminability (d′), criterion (c), and response bias (β).

Whereas accuracy reflects overall performance, signal detection measures allow for a more precise assessment of whether spatial expectations affect sensitivity to object identity or instead shift the decision threshold participants apply when responding under uncertainty.
Discriminability (d′) was examined to assess how effectively participants could distinguish target objects from non-targets as a function of spatial certainty and object placement.
Responses were categorized as hits, misses, correct rejections, or false alarms, from which hit and false alarm rates were computed for each participant and condition.

Discriminability was calculated as the difference between the z-transformed hit rate and false alarm rate, with higher values indicating greater sensitivity to object identity (Stanislaw & Todorov, 1999).

The central theoretical question in Experiment 2 was whether the Placement × Spatial Certainty interaction would appear in eye movement measures, as predicted by the earlyintegration account, or whether it would emerge primarily in behavioural recognition measures, as predicted by the later evidence-evaluation account.

In summary, Experiment 2 revealed a dissociation between eye movement and behavioral measures of object processing.
Object placement influenced eye movements broadly, with longer viewing times for objects in unexpected than expected locations, but this effect did not depend on spatial certainty.
In contrast, spatial certainty modulated the effect of placement on recognition performance, with the interaction emerging in accuracy and discriminability but not in response bias measures.

This pattern provides stronger support for the later evidenceevaluation account than for the early-integration account: the precision of object-location priors was not expressed as a selective high-certainty placement effect in eye movements, but instead shaped how object information was evaluated during recognition decisions.
Experiment 2 examined how spatial certainty and object placement jointly shape object processing across fixations and recognition decisions.

Building on prior work demonstrating parafoveal preview benefits in scenes, we asked whether the strength of object-scene spatial associations constrains the extraction and integration of visual information, particularly under conditions in which visual input is limited.

Within the framework outlined earlier, Experiment 2 tested two possibilities: the early-integration account, in which the Placement × Spatial Certainty interaction should appear in eye movement measures, and the later evidence-evaluation account, in which this interaction should emerge most clearly in recognition accuracy and sensitivity.
The results revealed a clear dissociation between eye movement measures and behavioral indices of performance.

Across eye movement measures, object placement exerted a strong influence on processing, such that objects appearing in unexpected locations elicited longer fixation durations regardless of their spatial certainty.

This finding suggests that spatial congruency broadly affects object processing once the object is fixated, likely reflecting the cost of resolving discrepancies between expected and observed object locations.
Critically, however, object placement did not interact with spatial certainty in these measures.
Thus, although unexpected placement increased viewing times, this cost did not depend on the precision of the spatial prior.
By contrast, spatial certainty played a central role in behavioural recognition performance.
Accuracy and discriminability both revealed Placement × Spatial Certainty interactions, whereas criterion and response bias did not.

Objects High in spatial certainty were recognized more accurately and with greater sensitivity when they appeared in Expected locations, suggesting that precise spatial priors helped participants evaluate the available object evidence more effectively when location information supported the target identity.

In contrast, objects Low in spatial certainty showed little or no reliable placement benefit, consistent with the idea that Expected and Unexpected locations are less diagnostic when spatial priors are more distributed.
Together, these findings indicate that the precision of object-location priors was expressed most clearly when participants evaluated available object evidence during recognition decisions.
The pattern for Low-Certainty objects also highlights an important distinction between the precision and flexibility of spatial priors.
Low-certainty objects do not lack spatial expectations; rather, their expected locations are more broadly distributed.
As a result, the Expected versus Unexpected Placement distinction may be less diagnostic for these objects.
This may explain why placement produced weaker behavioural effects for low-certainty objects than for high-certainty objects.
More speculatively, when low-certainty objects appear in unusual locations, observers may rely more heavily on the available object evidence because location provides less decisive constraint.

This interpretation is consistent with predictive-processing accounts in which the precision of priors determines how strongly prediction errors are weighted (Seriès & Seitz, 2013), but it should be treated cautiously because the present measures do not directly isolate prediction-error weighting.

text.text: Taken together, Experiment 2 provides stronger support for the later evidence-evaluation account than for the early-integration account.
Spatial congruency influenced eye movements broadly, but the precision of object-location priors did not modulate this effect during object viewing.
Instead, spatial certainty shaped how placement influenced recognition accuracy and sensitivity.
These findings suggest that precise spatial priors constrain object recognition primarily when observers evaluate limited visual evidence and make an explicit recognition decision.
The present study examined how the precision of object-location priors shapes object recognition in scenes.

Drawing on predictive-processing accounts of vision, we asked whether spatial certainty, which reflects the degree to which an object is reliably associated with a specific scene region, modulates object processing across fixations or instead has its strongest influence when observers evaluate and make recognition decisions.

Across two experiments, we examined behavioral indices of decision making and in the second experiment, used eye movements to ask whether the same effects were evident as object information was sampled parafoveally and after direct fixation.
Across both experiments, object placement exerted a strong influence on processing, with objects appearing in unexpected locations incurring consistent costs.
However, the influence of spatial certainty was more selective.

In Experiment 1, Spatial Certainty interacted with object Placement in behavioral measures of recognition, indicating that strong object-location priors supported recognition when objects appeared in Expected locations.
In Experiment 2, eye movement measures showed effects of Placement, but did not show corresponding Placement × Spatial Certainty interactions.
In contrast, behavioral measures again showed strong interactions between Spatial Certainty and Placement in accuracy and discriminability.

This pattern provides stronger support for the later evidence-evaluation account than for the early-integration account: spatial placement influenced object processing across fixations, but the precision of objectlocation priors was most clearly seen when observers evaluated the available visual evidence for recognition.
Bayesian model comparison reinforced this pattern, favouring interaction models for accuracy and discriminability but models without the interaction for reaction time and eye movement measures.
Together, these findings indicate that spatial context does not operate as a uniform facilitative cue.
Instead, its predictive power depends on the precision of the object-location prior, and this precision is expressed most clearly when observers evaluate limited object evidence for recognition.
A central contribution of the present study is to show that the predictive power of scene context depends on the precision of the object-location prior.
Prior work on scene context has often contrasted expected and unexpected objects or consistent and inconsistent object-scene relations (e.g., Biederman et al., 1982).
text.formatted: Prior work on scene context has often contrasted expected and unexpected objects or consistent and inconsistent object-scene relations (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Biederman et al., 1982)</ref>.

text.text: The present findings suggest that this distinction is incomplete.
Objects differ in how precisely their locations are predicted by the scene, and this variability determines how strongly placement constrains recognition.

Within predictive processing frameworks, prior knowledge is not only used to generate predictions about forthcoming sensory input; it also determines how incoming evidence is evaluated relative to those predictions (Friston, 2010; Seriès & Seitz, 2013).
text.formatted: Within predictive processing frameworks, prior knowledge is not only used to generate predictions about forthcoming sensory input; it also determines how incoming evidence is evaluated relative to those predictions <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Friston, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Seriès & Seitz, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: From this perspective, spatial certainty can be understood as an index of the precision of an object-location prior that modulates the impact of sensory evidence on object recognition and decision-making.
The behavioral results from both experiments are consistent with this precision-based account.

High-Certainty objects were recognized more accurately and with greater discriminability when they appeared in expected locations, suggesting that precise spatial priors increased the diagnostic value of placement during recognition.
When these objects appeared in unexpected locations, recognition was impaired, consistent with a cost of evaluating briefly sampled object evidence against a violated spatial expectation.

In contrast, Low-Certainty objects were less consistently constrained by Placement conditions, as expected if their spatial priors are more distributed and therefore provide weaker location-specific evidence.
When spatial expectations are diffuse, confirmation or violation carries less informational weight and perceptual decisions may rely more heavily on visual evidence.
The pattern for low-certainty objects also highlights that spatial certainty can influence decisions through the relative plausibility of the available alternatives.
When a high-certainty foil is spatially implausible, observers may be better able to reject it, increasing support for the lowcertainty target.
This precision-based interpretation also helps explain why Unexpected Placement had asymmetric consequences across object types.
For high-certainty objects, unexpected placement created a strong mismatch between the object and its typical location, reducing recognition accuracy and sensitivity.
For low-certainty objects, the same placement manipulation was less diagnostic because these objects are plausibly associated with multiple scene regions.
Thus, spatial certainty does not simply scale the magnitude of contextual facilitation.
Instead, it changes how spatial information is used when observers evaluate ambiguous or briefly available object evidence.
This allows perception to adapt flexibly to atypical configurations (Summerfield & de Lange, 2014).

text.text: By framing spatial certainty as the precision of an object-location prior, the present findings extend prior work on scene context and object recognition (Bar, 2004; Castelhano & Heaven, 2011; Seriès & Seitz, 2013).

text.text: Much of this literature has emphasized whether objects are semantically or spatially consistent with a scene.
The present results show that spatial consistency is not a uniform constraint: its effect depends on how strongly the object is tied to a particular location.
This notion is also seen in the Scene Grammar account of scene organization of both semantic and syntactic placement of objects.
Anchor objects (e.g., stove, bathroom vanity) within the scene structure carry precise spatial predictions for smaller associated objects (e.g., frying pan or soap).

Scene grammar as a framework offers a mechanism for why objects appear where they do and from there, we can infer differences in the predictability of the object's location (Boettcher, Draschkow, Dienhart & Võ, 2018; Draschkow & Võ, 2017; Võ et al., 2019; Võ, 2021).
text.formatted: Scene grammar as a framework offers a mechanism for why objects appear where they do and from there, we can infer differences in the predictability of the object's location <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Boettcher, Draschkow, Dienhart & Võ, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Draschkow & Võ, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Võ et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Võ, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: However, there is an interesting theoretical distinction: scene grammar treats spatial predictability as relational, in that it is derived from an object's position within an anchor-phrase hierarchy, whereas Spatial Certainty treats it as an object-level property that can be derived based on ratings of that object in isolation.
Thus, these accounts point to two complementary sources of variation of spatial placement of objects in scenes.

The current study further adds that this graded variability determines whether spatial context affects recognition as a broad placement cost or as a precision-dependent influence on behavioural sensitivity.
A central question raised by the present findings concerns when the precision of objectlocation priors affects object recognition.

The early-integration account predicted that spatial certainty and placement should interact in eye movement measures if precise spatial priors constrain object processing as information is sampled across fixations.
This prediction was not supported.
Instead, fixation durations were sensitive to placement, with objects in unexpected locations producing processing costs, but these placement effects did not depend reliably on spatial certainty.
Thus, spatial placement influenced object processing across fixations, but the precision of the object-location prior did not strongly affect eye movement measures.
This pattern is broadly consistent with fixation-control models that distinguish the timing of eye movements from the later evaluation of object and scene information.

According to the CRISP model (Nuthmann et al., 2010), fixation durations in scene viewing are governed by an autonomous timing mechanism that can be modulated by processing difficulty after fixation onset, rather than being fully determined by anticipatory predictions about upcoming objects.
text.formatted: According to the CRISP model <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Nuthmann et al., 2010)</ref>, fixation durations in scene viewing are governed by an autonomous timing mechanism that can be modulated by processing difficulty after fixation onset, rather than being fully determined by anticipatory predictions about upcoming objects.

text.text: The strong placement effects observed in the current study are consistent with the idea that unexpected object locations create general integration difficulty once the object is processed.

However, the absence of Placement × Spatial Certainty interactions suggests that the precision of object-location priors did not modulate this integration difficulty at the level of fixation durations.
Importantly, the absence of spatial-certainty interactions in eye movement measures should not be interpreted as evidence that spatial priors never guide attention.
For example, Krzyś et al. (2025) showed that spatial certainty can guide attention in visual search, where observers choose where to look among competing regions.
text.formatted: For example, <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Krzyś et al. (2025)</ref> showed that spatial certainty can guide attention in visual search, where observers choose where to look among competing regions.

text.text: In the present task, participants were directed toward a predefined target location, reducing the opportunity for spatial certainty to influence gaze allocation.
Thus, the present eye movement measures are best interpreted as indices of object processing once the relevant location had been fixated.

The dissociation of effects of precision on eye movement measures vs. recognition decision has a broader parallel in work distinguishing the grain of information at different points in a processing sequence.

This interpretation is consistent with work showing that extrafoveal information and contextual expectations can modulate fixation durations after sufficient processing time has elapsed (Antes, 1974; Rayner, 2009; Reingold & Glaholt, 2014).

text.text: Furthermore, in a recent study, Yu, Hanks and Geng (2022) found that initial attentional guidance draws on coarser, more relational target information, while subsequent decisions about whether a fixated object matches the target draws on more precise information.

text.text: The present eye movement measures index object processing after the target object has been selected, so the mapping onto their two stages is not direct.
However, the broader principle still applies, in that later, more deliberate judgments can be more sensitive to precise prior information than the processes that precede them.
So, the framework by Yu et al. (2022) offers a way to understand why spatial certainty shaped recognition decisions, but not object-processing eye movement measures.

text.text: Across studies, coarser and more precise information appear to influence processing at different temporal windows.
The behavioural findings provide stronger evidence for the later evidence-evaluation account.

Across both experiments, Spatial Certainty interacted with Placement in accuracy and discriminability (d′), indicating that the precision of object-location priors influenced how effectively observers identified the object.
In contrast, criterion and response bias showed little evidence of corresponding interactions.
Thus, Spatial Certainty appears to have affected recognition sensitivity, but does not appear to produce a general shift in the response threshold.
High-Certainty objects, suggesting that precise object-location priors increased the diagnostic value of the available visual evidence when expectations were confirmed.
In contrast, when spatial priors were weak, discriminability was less sensitive to object placement, suggesting that diffuse expectations exert fewer constraints on perceptual inference.

This asymmetry is consistent with predictive processing accounts in which the precision of prior beliefs determines not only perceptual weighting but also the downstream consequences of prediction errors (Friston, 2010; Seriès & Seitz, 2013).

text.text: Strong priors increase the informational value of both confirmation and violation.
When a high-certainty object appeared in its expected location, placement provided useful evidence for the object decision.
When it appeared in an unexpected location, the mismatch between the object and its typical location reduced recognition sensitivity.
For low-certainty objects, placement was less diagnostic because these objects are plausibly associated with multiple regions.
Thus, spatial certainty did not uniformly scale performance; it changed how much weight placement carried during recognition.
Importantly, these recognition effects help reconcile the dissociation observed between eye movement measures and behavioural performance.

Eye movement measures were better characterized by models without the Placement × Spatial Certainty interaction, whereas accuracy and discriminability showed that the impact of placement depended on the precision of the object-location prior.
This pattern suggests that spatial priors exerted their strongest influence when briefly sampled object information was used to determine object identity under uncertainty.

By incorporating signal detection measures into the analysis of scene perception, the present study shows that spatial knowledge affects not only whether objects are processed more easily, but also how diagnostic the available evidence is for recognition.

A central motivation for the present study was to ask whether spatial priors in scenes operate like predictability effects in reading (Rayner, 1998; Rayner et al., 2003), where parafoveal preview and contextual constraint influence subsequent processing.

text.text: The present findings suggest a more nuanced conclusion.
Spatial placement affected eye movements, indicating that object-location information influenced processing across fixations.
However, the precision of object-location priors did not produce the predicted Placement × Spatial Certainty interaction in eye movements.
Instead, that interaction emerged most clearly in recognition accuracy and discriminability.
This refines prior work showing that parafoveal object processing in scenes is modulated by higher-level scene context (e.g., Castelhano & Pereira, 2018).
text.formatted: This refines prior work showing that parafoveal object processing in scenes is modulated by higher-level scene context (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Castelhano & Pereira, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: The present study suggests that not all forms of contextual constraint are expressed in the same way.

Broad violations of expected placement may affect object processing across fixations, whereas the graded precision of an object's spatial prior may be most evident when observers evaluate limited visual evidence for recognition.
At the same time, the present findings leave open an important question about how spatial priors operate across the transition from parafoveal preview to foveal object processing.

Within a predictive-processing framework, parafoveal information may be used to generate an initial prediction about object identity or location, which is then updated once the object is directly fixated.
Spatial certainty provides a way to ask whether some object-location predictions are held with greater precision than others.
For high-certainty objects, a mismatch between expected placement and foveal input may require greater updating because the prior is more constrained.
For low-certainty objects, the same mismatch may be less costly because the prior is broader and can accommodate a wider range of locations.
Thus, the key issue for future work is not only whether parafoveal information is extracted, but how strongly it is weighted, maintained, or revised when new foveal evidence becomes available.
This question has clear parallels with the reading literature.

In reading, mismatches between parafoveal previews and subsequently fixated words produce processing costs, suggesting that information extracted before fixation is carried forward and revised when it conflicts with foveal input (Rayner et al., 2003).
text.formatted: In reading, mismatches between parafoveal previews and subsequently fixated words produce processing costs, suggesting that information extracted before fixation is carried forward and revised when it conflicts with foveal input <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Rayner et al., 2003)</ref>.

text.text: A similar mechanism may operate in scenes, but with an added source of complexity: object-location priors vary in precision.

Spatial certainty may therefore determine the cost of resolving inconsistencies between what is expected parafoveally and what is confirmed after fixation, either in terms of object identity, object location, or the relation between the object and the surrounding scene.

The present findings suggest that these costs may not always appear as early changes in fixation duration; instead, they may become most evident when observers must use briefly sampled visual information to identify an object.
The present task was not designed to fully isolate this updating process because eye movements were constrained by requiring participants to fixate the target object.
This likely reduced the opportunity for spatial priors to influence initial orienting or unconstrained gaze allocation.
This distinction may help explain why other studies have observed earlier effects of scene consistency on eye movements.

For example, Coco, Nuthmann, and Dimigen (2020) found that scene-consistent objects were fixated sooner and viewed for less time, whereas inconsistent objects produced longer fixation durations and increased viewing times.
text.formatted: For example, <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Coco, Nuthmann, and Dimigen (2020)</ref> found that scene-consistent objects were fixated sooner and viewed for less time, whereas inconsistent objects produced longer fixation durations and increased viewing times.

text.text: In contrast, the current paradigm directed gaze toward a predefined target location and limited object availability after fixation onset.
Under these conditions, spatial priors may have been less likely to affect where or when the eyes moved and more likely to affect how the available evidence was evaluated for recognition.
Future studies could more directly manipulate the relation between parafoveal and foveal object information.
For example, spatial certainty could be crossed with preview validity so that the parafoveal object either matches or conflicts with the object revealed after fixation.
This would allow researchers to test whether precise spatial priors affect the incorporation, discounting, or revision of parafoveal information when predictions are violated.

The target population is intended to be adult individuals, as we are interested in those who have experience with the types of indoor environments used in the stimuli (North American) and align with those who contributed to the spatial certainty ratings that define the High and Low Certainty conditions (Krzyś et al., 2025).

text.text: In this way, we intend the study to examine the precision of the priors we manipulated.
The participant sample was drawn from a university undergraduate population, which may have limited the generalizability of the findings to a broader demographic.
University students often share similar cognitive and perceptual characteristics, which might not reflect the diversity found in the general population.
Therefore, whether the findings are applicable across different age groups, educational backgrounds, and cultural contexts is an empirical question.
In sum, the present study shows that spatial regularities in scenes constrain object recognition in a graded and temporally specific manner.

Spatial placement broadly influenced object processing across fixations, but the precision of object-location priors, indexed by spatial certainty, determined whether placement altered recognition accuracy and sensitivity.

This pattern provides stronger support for a later evidence-evaluation account than for an earlyintegration account: spatial priors did not uniformly shape eye movement measures, but instead influenced how briefly sampled object information was used to determine object identity.
By treating spatial certainty as a measure of the precision of object-location priors, the present study extends predictive accounts of vision to the graded structure of scenes.

More broadly, these findings show that scene context is not a uniform source of facilitation; its influence depends on how reliably particular objects are associated with particular locations and on the stage of processing being measured.
